items.description_text: Youth work does not develop in isolation. It grows through cooperation, exchange of experience and shared reflection across different national contexts. New legislation, professional standards, competence frameworks, local youth centres and innovative forms of youth participation are emerging across the region. Practitioners and policy makers face common challenges: strengthening recognition of youth work, improving quality, creating sustainable support systems, responding to societal change, and ensuring that youth work remains relevant to young people's realities. At the same time, youth workers in Eastern Europe and Caucasus are responding to challenges such as armed conflicts, democratic resilience, migration, digital transformation, shrinking civic space, mental health, social cohesion and the participation of young people in rapidly changing societies. Their experience of building resilient youth work systems under rapidly changing circumstances offers valuable lessons not only for the region itself but also for youth workers across Europe seeking to strengthen the resilience of young people, communities and youth work structures in the twenty-first century. These developments create a unique opportunity for mutual learning. Rather than following a traditional capacity-building approach, this seminar is based on the principle that expertise exists in every participating country. It aims to create an equal partnership between participants. Instead of transferring ready-made models, participants will jointly explore how youth work can continue to grow while respecting different political, social and cultural realities. Aim To strengthen dialogue and cooperation between youth work practitioners, policy makers and supporting institutions from Erasmus+ Programme Countries, Neighbourhood East and Western Balkans in order to promote mutual learning and support the sustainable development, quality and recognition of youth work across Europe. items.description_text: The Spark: Understanding What Drives Youth Engagement is a four-day training course for youth workers, trainers, facilitators and others working in the field of non-formal learning and international youth work. Why do some young people actively participate while others stay on the side-lines? During the training, we will explore different factors that can influence young people’s engagement, including adolescent development, motivation, peer influence, sense of belonging, previous experiences, interests, competences and the social environment. We will also turn the focus towards ourselves as youth workers. We will reflect on what we consider to be passivity, what kind of participation we expect from young people, and how much real influence and ownership they have in the opportunities and activities we create for them. We will explore participation as something that develops over time and consider how young people can gradually build autonomy, responsibility, decision-making skills and ownership. The training will also examine what youth workers can realistically influence when supporting young people’s participation, how much control we are willing and able to share, and where the limits of our own role and responsibility lie. The programme is based on non-formal and experiential learning. Participants will connect the topics explored during the training with situations from their own practice and consider what they can understand or approach differently in their work. The Council of Europe and European Commission highlight that young people are currently experiencing and will continue to bear the brunt of worsening climate impacts, making climate action not only an environmental issue but a matter of intergenerational justice. Youth engagement is increasingly recognised as a decisive force in achieving Europe’s green transition. Both formal (school systems, civic participation structures) and informal (community projects, youth work) pathways empower young people to contribute to environmental action. The European Green Deal support initiatives emphasise that youth bring creativity, fresh perspectives, and a direct stake in long‑term climate solutions, making their involvement indispensable. The Council of Europe’s groundbreaking Recommendation on Young People and Climate Action stresses that young people must be meaningfully included in climate decision‑making processes. The recommendation highlights the need to protect young climate defenders, ensure access to rights, and remove structural barriers preventing youth from influencing policy. items.description_text: How do we break through the paralysis of crisis fatigue and reclaim our power to act in a world that feels increasingly out of our control? We are living through times of ecological, social, and political crisis. Geopolitical tensions, deep societal divisions, and environmental changes have created a heavy, exhausting sense of uncertainty. For many young people, this does not just cause worry—it leads to a deep feeling that nothing they do matters, causing them to fall into disengagement, frustration, and social withdrawal. But waiting for the uncertainty to pass is not an option. This training course is a direct call to move past passive concern and step into active, collective initiative. We start from the conviction that lasting change requires both inner transformation (shifting our emotional relationship to the crises we face) and systemic transformation (rebuilding collective will and trust in others). Education and youth work are the key levers for this dual change. We are gathering to address this state of being head-on, transforming crisis fatigue into a catalyst for community action. The training is delivered by the partnership behind Beyond the Frame, an Erasmus+ Cooperation Partnership in Youth (KA220-YOU) bringing together the Macedonian Association for Applied Psychology (North Macedonia), Idee in Movimento (Italy) and ArtéTeka (Ireland). It combines insights from art therapy, social psychology and non-formal education into a hands-on, practitioner-led experience. Who this is training for This offer is aimed specifically at people working in the field of non-formal learning and youth work: youth workers, educators, NGO staff, facilitators and volunteers who work directly with young people aged roughly 18-30. It is especially relevant to those supporting young people with fewer opportunities - including migrants, refugees, NEETs, and young people facing social or health-related barriers. No prior artistic or mental health training is required. Priority is given to participants who work with young people but have not had formal training in mental health, and who are looking for accessible, creative tools they can apply immediately in a non-formal setting. What you will learn By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Facilitate collage-based sessions that help young people express emotion, manage stress and build resilience Create safe, inclusive spaces using non-verbal methods that work across language and literacy barriers Guide young people from personal reflection toward civic dialogue and collective action Recognise and respond appropriately to emotional distress, and understand the boundary between youth work and therapy Apply and adapt the Beyond the Frame Toolkit

Across Greece, Cyprus, Bulgaria and Ireland, we reached out to the artists and community members who make these scenes come to life, diving deep into their experiences of belonging and community, identity and visibility, harassment and safety. This 90-minute online workshop shares what we found, but not in the way you'd expect. It is designed for those who want to strengthen their ability to support young people in understanding themselves, exploring career possibilities, and making realistic career decisions. The programme combines non-formal education, experiential learning, reflection, peer exchange, facilitation practice, and hands-on activities. Participants will work with methods and tools that can be directly adapted to their daily work with young people. The training will focus on: supporting young people in self-understanding and self-awareness; helping them identify their values, skills, and strengths; facilitating realistic career decision-making; dealing with uncertainty, decision anxiety, and information overload; supporting young people in moving from planning to action; strengthening resilience and adaptability; using non-formal methods, facilitation techniques, and digital tools in career guidance. The training is intended for youth workers, educators, social workers, counsellors, project coordinators, mentors, community leaders, and activists. YOUTH WORK CREATE will focus on the role youth work can play in challenging these limiting narratives and building a different mindset. The course approaches entrepreneurial spirit not simply as starting a business, but as a way of thinking and acting — being curious, taking initiative, recognising opportunities, solving problems, experimenting, learning from failure and having the confidence to turn ideas into action. It will also explore social entrepreneurship, encouraging young people to see challenges in their communities not only as reasons to leave, but also as opportunities to create solutions, services and positive local change. Participants will explore and test non-formal education techniques, methods and approaches for working with young people's mindsets: identifying and challenging stereotypes and limiting beliefs, discovering strengths and local resources, developing creativity and initiative, building resilience, exploring different career and entrepreneurial pathways, and moving from ideas towards action. Adults decide what is needed, what feels safe and what feels welcoming. But how often do we ask young people what they think? And more importantly, how often do we invite them to create these spaces with us? The idea for this training comes from a cocreation project in which four unaccompanied minors worked with judges, guardians and children's rights experts to redesign a courtroom for the Belgian Council for Alien Law Litigation. Their ideas helped create a space that felt calmer, clearer and more respectful. The project showed that when young people are treated as equal partners, everyone benefits, including the adults who use and work in these spaces. Why does this matter? The spaces young people use every day influence how they feel, act and connect with others. When they help shape these spaces, they build confidence, ownership and a stronger sense of belonging. At the same time, the whole community can benefit from spaces that better reflect the needs and experiences of the people who use them. Many STEAM activities start with a predefined outcome: build a bridge, create a vehicle, follow these instructions. Storybuilders Lab explores a different approach. The facilitator defines the learning intention, but participants influence the story, identify the problem and decide what needs to be created. The methodology follows a simple learning cycle: STORY → QUESTION → IDEAS → CHALLENGE → DESIGN → MAKE → TEST → IMPROVE → REFLECT → STORY CONTINUES Participants will learn how to use story triggers, mystery objects and open questions to generate curiosity and meaningful challenges. They will explore Story Democracy, a participatory method for collecting, combining and developing different ideas so that the direction of a project is not predetermined by the facilitator or dominated by the strongest voices in the group. A central part of the course is hands-on prototyping. Participants will work with accessible materials such as cardboard, recyclable materials and simple construction tools to turn ideas into physical prototypes. Makedo or similar cardboard-construction tools may be used where available, but no specialised equipment is required. The focus is not on creating a perfect final object. Participants practise an iterative process of: Make → Test → Notice → Change → Test again This allows them to explore how experimentation, “failure”, debugging and redesign can become valuable learning experiences in youth work. items.description_text: This Partnership Building Activity (PBA) consists of four days of interactive sessions and local visits where participants will have the opportunity to exchange good practices and strengthen networks with like-minded associations and organizations active in the Erasmus+ program. The idea is to gather organizations that want to expand their actions and implement new projects. There will be a balance between newcomer organizations and more experienced ones, in order to share proven methodologies, navigate common challenges, and foster peer-to-peer mentorship. Inspired by the concept of neural connectivity, this activity treats each organization as a key node in a dynamic European network. Just as neurons build stronger pathways through interaction, our aim is to spark active collaboration, combine fresh perspectives with proven experience, and turn creative synergies into real results. Over these four days, participants will focus specifically on forging strategic connections to co-create Erasmus+ Key Action 2 (KA2) partnerships in the Youth and Adult Education fields—leaving with concrete project ideas, trusted consortiums, and clear roadmaps for upcoming calls.

items.description_text: Humour is already present in youth work practice - but it's rarely used as a deliberate, structured tool. "Humour is Serious Business" (HiSB) is a 6-day Erasmus+ KA153-YOU training course (27 November - 3 December 2026, Hollókő, Hungary) that will help you turn something you probably already do instinctively into an intentional, ethical, and effective competence for engaging young people. This training is aimed specifically at practitioners in the field of non-formal learning and youth work - not at the general public. You should apply if you are a youth worker (professional or voluntary), a youth leader, a young person (18+) with leadership potential already identified by your organisation, or a practitioner with relevant expertise who works with young people (e.g. a coach, mentor or tutor), even if youth work is not your primary profession. Through non-formal methods - World Café, simulations and role play, clowning and improvisation, team building, and daily reflection groups - you will explore the many different types of humour, examine cultural differences in how humour is used, reflect on your own sense of humour, and develop concrete post-programme actions to bring back to your own community. Every participant leaves with a Personal Development Plan and the chance to earn a Youthpass. HiSB is delivered by an experienced international Training Team and hosted by MAVISZ (Hungary), together with partner organisations in Poland, Portugal, Armenia, Serbia, Latvia, Croatia, Montenegro and Spain. 36 participants will take part, 4 per sending country. Full details, including the daily programme, participant support structure, and reimbursement process, are in the Info Pack: https://mavisz.my.canva.site/hisb2026

items.description_text: Project Summary: Leveraging ICT and Social Media for Youth Inclusion and Participation Aim of the Project: The project is designed to equip youth workers with digital skills and tools to strengthen civic participation and engage young people through Information and Communication Technology (ICT). A core aim is to promote civic engagement through digital tools. Objectives: Strengthen Digital Competencies: Provide practical training in ICT, social media engagement, and digital content creation. Youth workers will be trained to guide young people in critical media analysis, recognizing misinformation, and using digital platforms for youth activism and community participation. Ensure Inclusion and Equal Access: Develop strategies to engage marginalized and disadvantaged young people who face barriers to digital participation. Encourage Innovation: Introduce interactive, gamified, and blended learning approaches to make digital engagement more dynamic and adaptive. Strengthen Transnational Cooperation: Establish a European Digital Youth Work Network for collaboration and knowledge exchange, and develop a Digital Civic Engagement Toolkit with practical resources. Outcome: The project aims to significantly enhance the digital skills of youth workers and strengthen youth engagement through the use of digital tools for non-formal education and social participation. It seeks to expand civic participation through youth-led activism and make digital youth work more accessible and inclusive for young people from diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds. The project's sustainability will be ensured through the creation of a European-wide network of digital youth workers and an open-access toolkit, ensuring that the methodologies remain relevant and scalable.

items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. Use storytelling and participatory methodologies to make heritage more relevant to young people. Encourage young people to question, reinterpret and remix heritage narratives. Besides our learnings, we also share the resources and approaches we have learned from within or outside of the field of youth work. More concretely, you will have a short glimpse into: - Experiential education - Solution focused approach - Trauma informed approach. items.description_text: How can international youth mobility become truly safe, inclusive, and empowering for Highly Vulnerable Young People? A course for youth workers, facilitators, and organisations to learn how to create safer, more inclusive, and trauma-informed international mobility experiences for Highly Vulnerable Young People (HVYP). This is a self-paced and practice-oriented online course for professionals working in youth mobility and non-formal education. The course supports participants in developing the competencies needed to responsibly include and support young people facing multiple and intersecting barriers in international programmes. You are going to learn about: safer and more inclusive mobility environments, safeguarding and risk management in practice, trauma-informed and solution-focused approaches, recognising and preventing harm and exclusion, supporting HVYP before, during, and after mobility experiences, professional boundaries, crisis response, and self-care in youth work. About this course International youth mobility projects can create powerful opportunities for learning, participation, connection, and personal growth. At the same time, for highly vulnerable young people, unfamiliar international environments may also involve increased vulnerability and risk. This course was developed within the LADDER project to support youth workers and organisations in creating mobility experiences that are not only accessible, but genuinely safe, supportive, and empowering. Through practical examples, case studies, reflection exercises, and field-tested approaches, participants will strengthen their capacity to: create safer and more inclusive mobility projects, anticipate and prevent risks, respond responsibly to challenging situations, and support young people facing multiple barriers. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition. The event will take place outdoors and is aimed at educators, activity leaders, and facilitators. In Brittany, 27 participants are expected.
